Assessment: show units, correctly evaluate the cases, and describe the limits of the simplified circuit model.

2.15.title: 2.15 Laboratory 2B — A plausible value from an inconsistent configuration

blocks.text: Objective: diagnose a range mismatch without equating a plausible signal with a valid measurement or a mismatch with malicious intent. Classification: offline analysis of synthetic records. Prerequisites: Sections 2.7–2.12. Topology: one transmitter, one AI, controller scaling, and a shared HMI/historian publication path, as in Figure 2.4.

Read scaling_cases.csv and the separate observation notes. For each case, calculate the transmitter current from the stated physical value and transmitter endpoints. Then calculate what the controller will report using its own endpoints. Identify cases where these numbers agree and disagree. Explain whether the analog current’s validity alone detects each problem.

For the investigation case, build a short chain of claims: observed number, source of that number, conversion applied, configuration evidence, independent physical observation, and remaining uncertainty. Do not insert the fixture’s “truth_level_m” into a proposed production detection. That field is supplied by the teaching scenario; a real installation requires an independently justified source.

Expected observations: matched ranges agree; a changed transmitter span can generate an in-range current that the controller interprets incorrectly. A stale HMI case is distinguishable from a fresh but mis-scaled value when trustworthy source timestamps are available. Common errors include treating an engineering workstation login as proof of a range change, assuming a historian is independent of its upstream source, and confusing an approved drawing with proof of the current configuration.

Reset: this exercise modifies no source record. Remove any optional generated output directory and start again from the unchanged fixtures. Assessment: the learner must correctly trace the arithmetic and provide a qualified conclusion that separates mechanism, consequence and attribution.

2.16.title: 2.16 Laboratory 2C — Device identity and evidence coverage

blocks.text: Objective: extend a small asset register into a tested collection plan. Classification: offline tabletop. Prerequisites: the equipment atlas and Section 2.13. Environment: assets.csv, evidence_manifest.csv and case_notes.md; these are fictional records constructed for this book, not captures from a customer or from the SANS classroom environment.

Build one record per physical or software role, but also record relationships: which input channel belongs to which controller, which transmitter feeds that channel, which HMI and historian share a source, and who approves instrument changes. Separate a human-friendly asset name from the verified manufacturer, family, order number, hardware revision and firmware. An asset named “Safety PLC” is not proof that the hardware, application or safety function is certified for its use.

For each investigation question, identify a data source, actual storage location, observed retention, clock basis, owner and one limitation. Mark capabilities as documented, configured, observed, or tested. A field that is unknown should remain unknown, with an assigned verification action; filling it with an attractive default makes the inventory less trustworthy.

Expected observations: the fixture contains a policy-versus-observed retention discrepancy, a shared upstream dependency, and an inventory item whose nickname suggests more than its verified identity supports. The correct response is to narrow claims and identify verification work, not to compensate with a larger list of unsupported fields.

Cleanup: none is required for the source files. Delete working copies created during the exercise. Assessment: produce a one-page CMF excerpt and an initial incident note that explains both what can be investigated and what cannot yet be resolved. Instructor solutions and a scoring rubric are in Book A.

Explain why a 24 V supply and a 3 V receiver drop are not contradictory. Calculate the current for a 0–6 m transmitter at 1.5 m. Explain why a four-wire RTD and a four-wire transmitter are not the same connection problem. Describe one way a pump can receive a valid command without producing flow.

A transmitter sends 12 mA and the HMI displays 50 percent. List the missing facts needed to interpret a physical level. Explain what a growing ingestion delay can and cannot tell you. Identify two evidence sources that can agree because they share a dependency. Describe the additional evidence needed before attributing a range mismatch to an unauthorised change.

An engineer proposes restoring yesterday’s configuration immediately. Identify the process, document-control and evidence-preservation questions that should be resolved before an authorised restoration. Then explain how a known benign event can test a CMF claim without conducting an uncontrolled experiment on a live plant.

A measurement is not just a number. It is a physical interaction, an electrical or digital representation, a configuration-dependent conversion, a quality and timing context, and an evidence trail. Correct arithmetic is necessary but insufficient: the endpoints, units, channel identity and source provenance also need to be correct.

The field device can be the origin of both a process value and a security-relevant configuration change. The controller can be working correctly on the wrong input. The HMI and historian can agree without independently corroborating the process. A collection plan becomes useful when its data and limitations have been tested, not merely listed.

The next chapter will turn these principles into instrument selection and drawing interpretation: pressure and temperature measurements, level and flow technologies, valve and drive assemblies, instrument tags, P&IDs, loop diagrams and I/O lists. The following equipment atlas provides concrete hardware examples before that deeper treatment.

E1.title: E1. A modular PLC: Siemens S7-1500 and the CPU 1511-1 PN

blocks.text: A programmable logic controller repeatedly acquires information, executes an engineered application and updates outputs or communications. The processor is only one part of a modular station. The surrounding assembly can include system and load power supplies, a backplane, communication interfaces, input/output modules, terminals, memory media and wiring. A controller’s engineering project describes more than the program: it also describes hardware, networks, tags and other configured resources.

The supplied ICS410 uses an Allen-Bradley modular PLC photograph to introduce that separation. It is useful because the physical modules are visible. The source does not identify the exact CPU in its prose, so this book does not invent an order number from the picture. Nor is that photograph labelled as a Siemens S7-1500. [S410.1, PDF 26, printed 24.]

For a specifically identified Siemens example, the official product catalogue describes CPU 1511-1 PN as an entry-level member of S7-1500 for applications with moderate program and processing requirements. It can serve central and distributed I/O through PROFINET; the catalogue describes an integrated two-port interface. A dated Siemens manual lists standard CPU article 6ES7511-1AL03-0AB0. These identifiers are useful for reading documentation, not a guarantee of compatibility with every project carrying the name “1511.” [V04, V05.]

In the tank example, a PLC could read level, apply the operating logic, calculate an outlet-pump demand and publish status to an HMI. The fictional control loop in Chapter 1 was not executed on this CPU. A real implementation needs a selected I/O module, compatible signal type, engineering-tool and firmware relationship, cycle/timing design, and an authorised validation process.

When examining an authorised cabinet photograph, locate the CPU label, power connections, removable media, status indicators, module order numbers and terminal labels. Do not infer the configuration or permissions from appearance. LEDs show selected device states; they are not a complete forensic record. Two Ethernet sockets also do not prove independent security interfaces or provide a firewall boundary.

For maintenance and recovery, distinguish the approved offline engineering project from the running application and from whatever a particular upload/export operation can retrieve. Record tool version, device support packages, firmware, hardware configuration, protected components and the tested restoration method. A folder named “PLC backup” is not enough to establish recoverability. Common diagnostic hypotheses include an I/O-channel problem, a configuration mismatch, an application fault, a power dependency and a communication failure; the process symptoms determine which to test first. [S410.1, PDF 26; S515.2, PDF 166, 177–185.]

E2.title: E2. A compact PLC: S7-1200 G2 CPU 1214C

blocks.text: Compact controllers combine a CPU with selected built-in functions and I/O in a small assembly, while allowing defined expansion. Compact does not mean nonindustrial, and modular does not automatically mean safety-rated. The application, exact hardware and certification scope matter more than the shape of the enclosure.

A concrete G2 example is CPU 1214C DC/DC/DC, article 6ES7214-1AH50-0XB0 in Siemens’ December 2024 ordering documentation. The same documentation lists AC/DC/relay and DC/DC/relay variants with different article numbers, and separately lists fail-safe CPU 1214FC variants. The slash-separated designations help distinguish supply and input/output arrangements, but the terminal diagram and ratings remain authoritative. They are not interchangeable purchase descriptions. [V06.]

The important migration lesson is particularly relevant to older course notes: Siemens explicitly states that S7-1200 G2 is not hardware-compatible with the previous S7-1200 family. Program conversion and hardware replacement are separate questions. A project that can be migrated does not make an old expansion module electrically or mechanically compatible with the new controller. [V07.]

The current product page also describes NFC-based access to diagnostic/device information and a web server/Web API. Those capabilities expand the inventory and access-control questions; they do not establish that a particular service is enabled, remotely exposed or unauthenticated. Record the actual enabled interfaces, physical access conditions and supported security configuration. [V07.]

As a teaching device, a compact PLC is attractive because a small process can be followed end to end. Nevertheless, the software-only tank simulator does not validate G2 instruction timing, actual I/O behaviour, hardware protection or firmware security. A later isolated hardware lab should use a documented bill of materials and a compatible engineering environment rather than instructions inherited from a different S7-1200 generation.

A useful exercise is to compare two inventory entries that both say “CPU 1214C.” One might be an older generation, another a G2; even within G2, different electrical variants exist. Before discussing an advisory or spare, require the complete article number, hardware revision, firmware and role. That is the difference between recognising a product name and knowing which device is actually present.

E3.title: E3. Remote I/O: Siemens ET 200SP with an IM 155-6 interface

blocks.text: Remote I/O moves the electrical connection point closer to field devices while a higher-level controller performs the associated application logic. A station can contain an interface module, several signal modules, terminal/base units and power distribution. It is an important asset even when no separate general-purpose control program runs in its head module: losing the station can remove several measurements or commands at once.

Siemens describes ET 200SP as a modular IP20 I/O system. Its interface variants include IM 155-6 PN for PROFINET, IM 155-6 DP for PROFIBUS, and IM 155-6 MF for supported MultiFieldbus connectivity. The family also includes controller-based head-end alternatives, so a photograph of narrow ET 200SP modules does not by itself tell you whether the station is only remote I/O or contains a controller. [V08.]

Imagine that six transmitters share a remote cabinet. The IP address may identify the station interface, while each transmitter remains a separate physical process asset with its own tag, range, calibration and wiring. A network-discovery result can therefore undercount the equipment that matters. The asset model should retain both the station and its channel-to-instrument relationships.

Fault analysis must distinguish the network path, the station interface, individual signal modules, field supply groups and field wiring. A reachable interface with several bad channels is not the same problem as an unreachable station. Replacement also requires more than matching a module’s width: signal type, base unit, potential group, channel configuration, version compatibility and configured loss-of-communication behaviour must be checked from the actual documentation.

For monitoring, channel diagnostics and controller events may be more useful than packets alone. Ask whether the system exports module faults, parameter changes and station failures, and test what the receiving system actually stores. Do not infer a universal syslog interface for remote I/O. The collection framework should show the controller or engineering system through which such evidence is available. [S410.1, PDF 31–33; S515.2, PDF 177–185.]

E4.title: E4. A DCS controller: ABB AC 800M and PM866A

blocks.text: A distributed control system, or DCS, is an integrated control-system architecture and engineering/operations ecosystem, not merely a different colour of PLC. It commonly combines controller applications, operator interaction, alarms, historical information, engineering tools and defined lifecycle workflows. The boundary with PLC-based systems overlaps; do not use a slogan such as “PLCs are only for discrete processes” to classify every installation. The supplied ICS410 introduces DCS and PLCs separately while noting modern overlap. [S410.1, PDF 25–26, printed 23–24.]

ABB’s AC 800M family is a rail-mounted modular controller platform with CPU, communication, power and accessory components. The official family description lists processors including PM866A and distinguishes variants by characteristics such as memory, redundancy support and safety-related scope. The family page must not be interpreted as certifying every CPU, application and installation for the same safety use. [V09.]

In a process-unit example, an AC 800M controller could participate in the control portion of an 800xA system, while operator and engineering functions reside in other components. The unit’s control logic, I/O configuration, communication interfaces and operator representations need a consistent engineered relationship. A server problem and a controller problem can therefore have different immediate process consequences.

The asset description should identify the CPU and communication modules, the I/O architecture, any redundant partner, the engineering environment and the process units served. Redundancy needs a dependency map: two controllers can share field instruments, power sources, cabinets, networks or configuration errors. Duplication alone is not independence.

A useful troubleshooting scenario is a restored engineering workstation whose project opens correctly but no longer matches the installed libraries, firmware or communications configuration. The recovery question is not just whether the project file exists. It is whether the complete required environment is controlled and whether a restoration has been validated for the exact system. The later ABB deep-study chapter will examine version-specific engineering and diagnostics rather than assume one workflow across all installed generations.

The earlier Iran map contains project evidence for ABB technologies, including migration contexts. It does not verify that PM866A is the processor installed at those sites. Keep “ABB family relevance” and “verified site model” as different evidence fields. [R20, R26; V09.]

Pressure instruments connect the process to a measurement system. They do not simply “read a pressure number from the network.” The process connection, sensing arrangement, wetted materials, mounting, configured range and environmental limits all affect whether the measurement is appropriate.

Emerson’s Rosemount 3051 family includes inline and coplanar arrangements. The verified manufacturer image linked below is a 3051T inline product illustration; it is not a 3051C differential-pressure assembly. The family supports several communication/output options, but a specific ordered transmitter does not necessarily contain every option on the family page. [V01.]
Manufacturer photograph: Rosemount 3051T inline transmitter
Manufacturer technical reference: Rosemount 3051 family

The distinction between gauge, absolute and differential pressure must precede a device choice. Gauge pressure is referenced to local atmospheric pressure; absolute pressure is referenced to vacuum; differential pressure compares two pressures. A pressure-based level calculation then introduces additional process assumptions, including fluid density and the pressure reference at the tank surface.

For a fictional open tank of water with density assumed constant at 1,000 kg/m³, a 2 m height corresponds to hydrostatic pressure of rho × g × h = 1,000 × 9.81 × 2 = 19,620 Pa, or 19.62 kPa. This is a physical teaching calculation, not a configured range or installation instruction for a 3051. A pressurised vessel, varying density, impulse-line arrangement or remote seal can require a different measurement model.

Ordinary problems can include an unsuitable range, an incorrect pressure reference, a plugged sensing path, trapped gas or liquid in a relevant impulse arrangement, environmental effects or configuration mismatch. Do not infer an adversary from a physically implausible level until the measurement method is understood.

The security-relevant record should connect device identity to the process tag, configured endpoints, units, damping, output option, device-access methods and approved changes. Depending on generation and option, diagnostics may help investigate loop or sensing problems; availability and exported evidence must be checked for the exact unit. The SOC should not assume that a HART-capable instrument’s configuration changes are visible in ordinary Ethernet monitoring. [V01, V11.]

A temperature transmitter is not the same object as the temperature-sensing element. The element responds to temperature; the transmitter interprets its electrical behaviour and exposes a configured measurement to another system. Sensor type, connection method and configuration have to agree. A physically connected sensor can produce a wrong value when interpreted using the wrong sensor model.

The Rosemount 3144P is a real transmitter family for temperature applications. Emerson describes a dual-compartment housing, sensor diagnostics, and options including dual-sensor/Hot Backup and X-well-related applications. These are product-family capabilities, not assertions that every installed 3144P has the same sensors, options or configuration. [V02.]
Manufacturer photograph: Rosemount 3144P
Manufacturer technical reference: Rosemount 3144P family

A resistance temperature detector changes resistance with temperature; a thermocouple uses a thermoelectric voltage relationship and requires the appropriate reference-junction treatment. The wire-count discussion in Chapter 2 is therefore not cosmetic. Lead compensation for an RTD and the power/output wiring of its transmitter are separate design questions.

For a fictional 0–200 degrees Celsius transmitter, 12 mA represents 100 degrees Celsius under our linear mapping. That arithmetic does not reveal whether the correct sensor type is configured or whether the sensor is in good thermal contact with the process. A correct current-loop calculation can coexist with a poor physical measurement.

Common investigation questions include whether one sensor or multiple sensors are used, which value is published, whether fallback or backup behaviour is configured, and how faults are represented downstream. Two inputs in one housing are not automatically independent safety measurements. The CMF should record which diagnostics are actually collected, not merely those listed in a brochure.

A practical first learning route is to read a sensor-connection diagram, identify the transmitter’s separate output interface, and analyse supplied configuration records without connecting to equipment. Changing a sensor type or range on a production transmitter can change control behaviour; it is an engineering change, not a harmless way to test a security tool. [V02; S410.1, PDF 31–33.]

E7.title: E7. A valve positioner: Fisher FIELDVUE DVC6200

blocks.text: A control-valve assembly can include a valve body, trim, an actuator, accessories and a positioner. The valve body affects fluid flow. The actuator creates motion. The positioner compares a demand with position feedback and regulates the actuator interface. A solenoid used for a particular protective or operating function is another component, not a synonym for the entire assembly.

Emerson describes the Fisher FIELDVUE DVC6200 as a HART-communicating digital valve controller with linkage-less feedback. It is a positioner/control instrument, not a complete valve body and actuator. Available diagnostics and integration depend on the selected product and application. [V03.]
Manufacturer photograph: Fisher FIELDVUE DVC6200
Manufacturer technical reference: DVC6200

In a fictional flow-control loop, the process controller might request more valve opening. The positioner’s local feedback can help move the actuator toward the requested travel. But 50 percent travel is not necessarily 50 percent flow. Valve characteristics, pressure conditions and the wider process determine the flow relationship. Treating these numbers as interchangeable creates both tuning and investigation errors.

A valve that does not reach demand can have mechanical, pneumatic, electrical, configuration or process causes. Examples include sticking, inadequate actuator supply, travel limits, a feedback issue or an unsuitable configured relationship. Diagnostics may narrow the possibilities; they do not eliminate the need for process and maintenance expertise.

Never infer fail-open or fail-closed behaviour from the positioner brand. The complete assembly and its engineered application determine what happens under specified losses of power, air or signal. A protective-system role needs separate approved documentation. The relevant inventory therefore includes the valve tag, actuator type, positioner identity, control demand path, feedback path, supply dependencies and authorised settings. [V03; S410.1, PDF 31–33.]

E8.title: E8. A variable-speed drive: ABB ACS880-01

blocks.text: A drive converts electrical power into a controlled supply for a motor. It is not the motor, pump or process itself. In a pump application, the controller may issue a speed demand to the drive, the drive controls the motor’s electrical behaviour, and the motor moves the pump shaft. A displayed frequency or speed demand does not independently confirm delivered fluid flow.

ABB identifies ACS880-01 as a wall-mounted member of the ACS880 industrial-drive family. The manufacturer describes direct torque control and configurable integration options, including fieldbus connectivity. The broad family spans different ratings and options, so a complete type code and option list are necessary before applying an installation manual, spare-part decision or advisory. [V10.]
Manufacturer illustrated product reference: ACS880-01

A useful conceptual chain is controller demand → selected drive control source → drive control algorithm → motor → pump → flow. The selected control source matters. A local control-panel mode can behave differently from a remote terminal or fieldbus mode. An investigator must establish which source currently owns the command before interpreting a network record as the effective demand.

In a fictional case, the network speed command changes but the motor does not respond. Plausible explanations include the drive operating in local control, an active limitation, a drive fault, a disabled enable/permissive path, a communications mapping problem or a mechanical load issue. A packet showing a requested value does not choose among them.

Recovery should preserve the drive’s approved parameter set, motor/application data, option configuration, firmware identity and tested restoration procedure. A generic factory reset is not a safe restoration strategy for a process drive. Safety-related drive functions, where present, must be treated within their documented safety application; a software state or safety-function label is not permission to work on an energised motor circuit. [V10; S410.2, PDF 136, printed 59.]

E9.title: E9. An HMI panel: Siemens MTP700 Unified Comfort

blocks.text: An HMI is the operator’s interaction and presentation layer. It can display measurements, alarms, trends and selected commands, but it does not thereby become the source of every control decision. Some applications distribute logic across several components, so the actual engineering design must be checked instead of assuming that all logic resides in either the PLC or the panel.

Siemens’ Unified Comfort documentation identifies MTP700 as a seven-inch panel in that family. “MTP700” alone is not a sufficient inventory description because a Unified Basic family also contains an MTP700. The family designation and full order number matter alongside the software/runtime relationship. [V12, V13.]
Manufacturer technical reference: MTP700 Unified Comfort

A well-designed teaching screen should make stale or bad-quality information distinguishable from a valid measurement. Colour alone is insufficient. The displayed units, range, source age and operating mode should also be interpretable. A trend showing a flat line could mean a stable process, a frozen source, suppressed recording or presentation behaviour; the application’s acquisition and storage settings determine what evidence remains.

A panel’s project, runtime configuration, users, certificates where applicable, network settings and recovery method belong in the asset record. Determine which logs are available and which are actually exported. Do not assume that every HMI emits a standard syslog record for every operator action.

A common recovery mistake is to restore an HMI application without validating tag connections and scaling against the current controller project. The screen may look familiar while reading a different tag or applying an old conversion. The fault-isolation exercise in Chapter 2 therefore treats the HMI as one stage in the evidence chain, not as an unquestionable display of truth. [S410.1 supervisory-systems section; S515.2, PDF 177–185.]

E10.title: E10. An industrial managed switch: Moxa EDS-4008

blocks.text: An industrial switch forwards network frames between connected devices. Its purpose differs from the controller that executes process logic and from a firewall that enforces a specified security policy. Rugged construction, redundant power inputs and a ring-recovery feature are useful attributes, but they do not independently establish a secure architecture.

Moxa’s EDS-4008 series contains eight-port managed-switch variants with different combinations of copper, fibre, gigabit uplinks and Power over Ethernet options. A suffix is therefore part of the identity, not a decoration. The manufacturer’s support listing includes a June 2026 data sheet and separate operating-system documentation; matching the installed firmware to the correct manual matters. [V14.]
Manufacturer illustrated product reference: EDS-4008 series

For a fictional remote cabinet, the switch may connect the PLC, remote I/O interface, HMI and an uplink. An incorrect VLAN, port state, loop, fibre selection or redundancy configuration can disrupt that cabinet. If two power inputs originate from the same upstream supply, the apparent redundancy has a common dependency. The network drawing should preserve those details.

For a SOC, the attractive functions are not just packet forwarding. Configuration access, port state, time configuration and available event/management records can help explain a disturbance. However, the CMF must verify which features the exact switch supports, what is enabled, which fields arrive, and how long they are retained. Do not invent field names from another vendor’s syslog format.

Port mirroring is useful but is not a promise of complete, lossless visibility. Oversubscribed mirrors, missing traffic directions and traffic outside the observation point can create gaps. Configuring a mirror or inserting monitoring equipment also changes the engineered environment and must be authorised. Monitoring deployment is not automatically risk-free merely because the eventual sensor observes rather than controls the process. [S515.2 visibility and network-mapping sections; V14.]

E11.title: E11. An RTU: Siemens SICAM A8000 CP-8050

blocks.text: A remote terminal unit supports telecontrol and automation, often connecting geographically separated process or electrical assets to supervisory systems. Its local functions and communications can overlap with PLC capabilities. The useful distinction is the engineered role, interfaces and operating requirements, not an absolute claim that one device type can or cannot perform local logic.

The supplied ICS410 uses a generic RTU architecture illustration. Siemens ProductCERT describes SICAM A8000 RTUs as modular devices for telecontrol and automation in energy supply. CP-8050 is a specific processor/controller example within that family. [S410.1, PDF 50, printed 48; V15.]

An RTU at a fictional substation might exchange status and supervisory commands with a control centre while interfacing with local devices. That does not mean every command travels directly through it, or that the protection system depends on the control-centre connection. The actual control and protection dependencies need to be drawn separately.

The device record should include exact processor hardware, firmware package, communication modules, enabled protocols, time source, approved configuration, remote-access path and local maintenance access. A complete identifier can materially change an advisory decision. The worked example following the atlas demonstrates a case where updating firmware alone is not the complete remedy.

Do not practise by probing a public RTU or replaying live control traffic. A first learning route is to study an offline configuration, read a manufacturer’s architecture description, classify captured laboratory messages and build a dependency map. An eventual simulator or hardware lab must state which functions it actually models. [V15; S515.2 asset-identification and visibility sections.]

E12.title: E12. A protection IED: Siemens SIPROTEC 7SJ85

blocks.text: An intelligent electronic device in a power-system context can implement protection, measurement, control and recording functions. A protection relay assesses electrical conditions according to its engineered settings and can participate in a trip scheme. It is not simply an IT relay that forwards messages, and its trip output is not the same thing as proof that a circuit breaker opened.

Siemens describes SIPROTEC 7SJ85 as an overcurrent-protection device for feeders, lines and capacitor banks, with a modular structure and the DIGSI 5 engineering environment. Its functions and I/O depend on the actual configuration. This is a real product example, not a statement that 7SJ85 is the most common relay in Iran. [V16.]
Manufacturer illustrated product reference: SIPROTEC 7SJ85

A beginner should distinguish measured current/voltage inputs, configured protection logic, a trip request, the trip circuit, the breaker mechanism and breaker-position feedback. Those stages can fail differently. An engineering change to a protection setting can alter the response to a real electrical fault, even when every network connection remains healthy.

The supplied ICS410 characterises some smart field-device logic as fixed. Treat that as a simplifying description, not a universal rule for all modern IEDs. The manufacturer’s documented engineering and configuration functions matter. For a security assessment, ask what settings and logic are configurable, which interfaces permit the change, what authority is required and what evidence is retained. [S410.1, PDF 34, printed 32; V16.]

A suitable first exercise is to classify an offline event timeline and identify what evidence would establish a setting change, a protection pickup, a trip command or a confirmed breaker transition. Do not infer all four from one log entry. Actual protection-setting design, testing and approval require qualified electrical/protection engineering and are outside the authority conferred by this course.

E13.title: E13. Worked advisory — Why the hardware revision belongs in the inventory

blocks.text: Siemens advisory SSA-128393, dated 10 December 2024, concerns firmware confidentiality in SICAM A8000 CP-8031/CP-8050. It describes a physical-access prerequisite and states that affected CPCI85 firmware versions below V05.30 need updating. Crucially, its additional information requires specified hardware variants to be revision JJ or later for the update to be effective. Both hardware and firmware conditions matter. [V15.]

The cited variants include CP-8050 6MF28050AA00 and the conformal-coated 6MF28050AC00, along with the corresponding CP-8031 variants. This is a bounded advisory about identified hardware and firmware, not proof of a remotely exploitable command path or a demonstrated power outage.

For an original tabletop example, compare two fictional inventory records. Both say CP-8050 and both list firmware V05.30. Record A documents hardware revision HH. Record B documents JJ. A check that evaluates only firmware would treat them alike, while the advisory requires different conclusions. If the hardware revision is unknown, the proper result is “verification required,” not “not affected.”

The exercise is entirely documentary. No physical probing or exploitation is required. The engineering response should confirm the exact asset and application, assess exposure and consequence, preserve configuration and recovery material, and plan any necessary work under authorised change control. The lesson is broader than this one vulnerability: family name, firmware and hardware revision are separate dimensions of applicability.

E14.title: E14. What to capture during a supervised equipment walkthrough

blocks.text: Start with the process function and responsible engineer, not a shopping list of labels. Record the tag and role, then the verified manufacturer, family, order/type code, hardware revision, firmware and options. Note how identity was established: a legible approved photograph, configuration export, maintenance record or a documented passive observation can support different levels of confidence.

Next trace signal, power and communication relationships. Identify the source of a measurement, the channel and scaling location, the actuator demand path, feedback, shared supplies, engineering access and time sources. Record the approved source of truth for configuration and the evidence needed to validate a restoration.

Finally connect the asset to a question in the CMF: what activity or failure do we need to detect, which record should show it, where does that record reside, and has its collection been tested? Leave unknown fields explicit. An accurate small inventory with process relationships is more useful than a large spreadsheet of guesses. [S515.2, PDF 166 and 177–185.]
